overview: American Tower is a global REIT that owns, operates, and develops multitenant communications real estate, primarily wireless towers, leasing space to mobile carriers and other tenants under long-term contracts with built-in escalators. Following the 2021 CoreSite acquisition, the company also operates a network of interconnection-dense data centers serving cloud, enterprise, and AI workloads. AMT operates roughly 149,000 communications sites across the United States, Latin America, Africa, and Europe (having exited India in 2024), plus about 27 CoreSite data center facilities concentrated in major U.S. metros.

business_model.summary: AMT leases vertical real estate (tower space) to multiple wireless carriers on the same structure, generating high-margin, highly recurring rental income with contractual annual escalators (~3% in the U.S., often CPI-linked internationally) and multi-year (5-10 year) tenant lease terms with high renewal rates. A smaller but faster-growing data center (CoreSite) segment leases colocation, interconnection, and cloud on-ramp capacity to enterprises, cloud providers, and AI infrastructure companies.

revenue_streams.name: U.S. & Canada property (tower leasing)
revenue_streams.trend: stable, low-single-digit organic growth ex-DISH churn

revenue_streams.name: International property (Latin America, Africa, Europe)
revenue_streams.trend: mixed - Africa growing double digits, Latin America declining on churn/FX

revenue_streams.name: Data centers (CoreSite)
revenue_streams.trend: growing double digits (~13-15% in 2026), accelerating on AI demand

revenue_streams.name: Services (site development, installation)
revenue_streams.trend: stable, tied to carrier capex cycles

business_model.customer_type: B2B - major wireless carriers (T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon domestically; regional/national carriers internationally) plus enterprise, cloud, and AI customers at CoreSite
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S. & Canada ~45% of property revenue, Latin America ~15-18%, Africa ~10%, Europe ~5-7%, with the balance from data centers; India exited in September 2024

main_competitors: Digital Realty and Equinix (data center segment)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the three dominant U.S. tower operators (with Crown Castle and SBA), collectively controlling roughly 70% of privately owned U.S. tower sites; largest global tower portfolio by site count and geographic diversification, with a growing niche position in interconnection-focused data centers via CoreSite

moat_factors.factor: High barriers to new tower construction
moat_factors.description: Zoning, permitting, and community opposition make new tower builds slow and costly, protecting incumbents' existing site locations
Multiple carriers colocate on the same tower; relocating equipment is expensive and disruptive, driving high tenant retention and pricing power on renewals
Largest global portfolio provides negotiating leverage with multinational carriers and diversifies country-specific regulatory/FX risk

moat_factors.factor: Contractual escalators and long lease terms
moat_factors.description: Built-in rent escalators (~3% U.S.) and 5-10 year initial terms provide highly visible, inflation-linked cash flows
Dense on-net customer ecosystems at key CoreSite facilities create network-effect-like stickiness for cloud on-ramps and AI infrastructure tenants

weaknesses: Customer concentration - revenue is highly dependent on a handful of large wireless carriers per market
Emerging-market exposure creates counterparty risk (e.g., Colombia's WOM bankruptcy, historical Vodafone Idea non-payment risk in India)
High leverage typical of tower REITs limits balance sheet flexibility versus data-center-pure-play peers
CoreSite scale still small relative to hyperscale data center operators (Digital Realty, Equinix), and land-constrained facilities limit total expansion capacity within existing footprint

growth_drivers: 5G network densification and rising mobile data consumption, with carriers expecting U.S. network capacity needs to roughly double by 2030
Emerging 6G, new mid-band/C-band spectrum deployment, and AI-driven wireless traffic supporting continued colocation and amendment activity

CoreSite data center expansion, with record leasing driven by AI/cloud workloads - nine of the top 10 AI companies and three of the top five neoclouds are deployed in CoreSite facilities; development pipeline positioned to roughly triple existing capacity
International tower builds and network investment in Africa (high-single to double-digit growth) as carriers expand coverage in underpenetrated markets
Portfolio optimization - proceeds and reduced risk from the 2024 India exit redeployed toward higher-return U.S. towers and data centers
Capital allocation shift toward debt paydown and buybacks ($1.6B remaining authorization) as growth capex needs moderate post-CoreSite integration

business.description: DISH defaulted on tower rent (~2% of total, ~4% of U.S. & Canada property revenue in 2025); Chapter 11 filing in 2026 stripped roughly $200M in annual U.S. revenue from the run rate and triggered 170+ lawsuits industry-wide over lease terminations
Multi-year decommissioning of overlapping Sprint sites has weighed on U.S. organic growth; expected to substantially wind down through 2026 but still a drag
Further wireless industry consolidation (fewer, larger tenants) would concentrate counterparty risk and could reduce total addressable colocation demand

Colombian carrier WOM's bankruptcy-like proceedings and ongoing AT&T Mexico rent arbitration have pressured Latin America organic growth (management guides -3% in 2026) and required incremental reserves (~$36M EBITDA / $33M AFFO impact)

financial.description: REIT structure combined with tower/data-center capex requires substantial debt; total debt around $37B against ~$63B total assets, making refinancing costs and covenant headroom a continual focus

Meaningful share of revenue and EBITDA generated in Latin American, African, and European currencies; 2026 guidance raises were partly driven by favorable FX rather than core operating improvement, a tailwind that could reverse

As a capital-intensive REIT, AMT's valuation and cost of capital are sensitive to long-term Treasury yields; rising rates have historically pressured the stock and raised the discount rate applied to its cash flows

regulatory.description: Local and national permitting processes affect the pace of new site construction, though this also acts as a barrier to entry favoring incumbents
Must continue to meet IRS REIT distribution and asset tests; any adverse change to REIT tax treatment would be a significant structural risk
FCC decisions on spectrum sales/reallocation (a factor cited in the DISH/EchoStar situation) can trigger tenant network decommissioning that hits tower lease revenue

macro.description: Africa and Latin America operations are exposed to currency devaluation, inflation, and political instability affecting both revenue translation and local carrier solvency
Wireless carrier capital spending is cyclical and tied to their own balance sheet health and spectrum auction outcomes; a slowdown reduces new colocation and amendment activity
CoreSite's growth acceleration is tied to sustained AI/cloud capital spending; a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment would directly affect the fastest-growing segment

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global tower industry outlook remains constructive, underpinned by rising mobile data consumption, 5G mid-band densification, early 6G planning, and new spectrum deployment; industry executives widely cite the current period as having multiple simultaneous demand catalysts (5G densification, 6G, spectrum, AI traffic) for the first time in years. Data center/colocation demand for AI and cloud workloads is a separate, faster-growing tailwind for the CoreSite segment.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - tower leasing is relatively defensive with contractual, escalator-driven recurring revenue, but new colocation/amendment activity is tied to carrier capex cycles, and the international segments (Latin America, Africa) carry higher macro/currency cyclicality
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - as a leveraged, capital-intensive REIT, AMT's equity valuation multiple and financing costs are sensitive to long-term interest rates; rate increases have historically driven underperformance versus the broader market
key_input_costs: Steel and construction materials for new tower builds
Financing/interest costs on variable and refinanced debt

recent_developments.event: Beat estimates with adjusted EPS of $1.86 and property revenue up 6.3% YoY to $2,688M; CoreSite data center revenue grew 13.4% YoY with record quarterly leasing, exceeding all of 2021's new business in a single quarter

Raised full-year 2026 guidance for the second time: property revenue to ~$10,770M (~5% YoY growth), Adjusted EBITDA to ~$7,275M, AFFO/share to ~$11.08 (~3% reported / ~5% FX-neutral ex-DISH growth); data center revenue growth guidance raised to ~15% from ~13%

DISH Wireless/EchoStar defaulted on tower rent obligations and subsequently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, removing DISH from organic growth calculations as of January 1, 2026 and stripping roughly $200M of annualized U.S. revenue; triggered extensive tower-industry litigation (170+ lawsuits) over lease decommissioning

Latin America organic tenant billings guided down (~-3%) on elevated churn, contract renegotiations, and capex cuts; incremental reserves taken for Colombian carrier WOM's bankruptcy-like proceedings (~$36M EBITDA / ~$33M AFFO impact); AT&T Mexico rent-escalation arbitration remains unresolved with ~$70M held in escrow provisions

Completed approximately $567.6M in share buybacks with $1.6B of board-authorized capacity remaining; issued new €750 million 4.000% notes and extended credit facilities to smooth the debt maturity profile
Raised quarterly dividend to $1.79/share (yield ~4% as of Q3 2026), reflecting confidence in underlying cash flow generation despite DISH and Latin America headwinds

Management characterized 2026 as a growth 'trough' year (masked in reported guidance by FX tailwinds) before an anticipated reacceleration from 5G densification, 6G, and AI-driven traffic in 2027 and beyond

items.notes: Raised by ~$110M at the midpoint; implies ~5% YoY growth reported, ~6% cash FX-neutral growth ex-DISH
~2% YoY reported growth, ~5% cash FX-neutral growth ex-DISH
~3% YoY reported growth, ~5% FX-neutral growth ex-DISH; second guidance raise of 2026
Raised from prior ~13% guide on sustained double-digit AI/cloud-driven leasing momentum; fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth

items.notes: DISH removed from organic growth base as of January 1, 2026; underlying growth composed of ~2.5% new leases/amendments plus escalators

items.notes: Reflects elevated churn, WOM (Colombia) reserves, and contract renegotiations; management expects weak Latin America growth to persist through 2027
Management's standing framework for steady-state tower organic growth once DISH/Sprint churn fully anniversary

guidance.management_commentary: Management described 2026 as a growth trough obscured by favorable currency translation, with confidence that Sprint-related churn substantially winds down during the year while DISH terminations create a new, separate headwind. Leadership emphasized four simultaneous demand catalysts for towers (5G densification, new spectrum, 6G, and AI-driven traffic) and highlighted CoreSite's record leasing quarter and AI/cloud customer wins as the primary driver of the guidance raise, while flagging Latin America (WOM bankruptcy, AT&T Mexico arbitration) as an area of continued caution through 2027.

bull_case: CoreSite data center segment is compounding at double-digit growth (~15% guided for 2026) on AI and cloud infrastructure demand, with a development pipeline that could roughly triple capacity and diversify AMT beyond pure tower leasing

Structural, multi-year tower demand tailwinds (5G densification, new spectrum, emerging 6G, rising mobile/AI data traffic) support durable mid-single-digit organic tower growth once Sprint and DISH churn fully anniversary
High barriers to new tower construction and colocation switching costs preserve pricing power and tenant retention, underpinning highly visible, escalator-driven recurring cash flows

Management is actively deleveraging and returning capital (dividend hikes, ~$1.6B buyback capacity remaining) after completing the India exit and moderating growth capex, improving balance sheet flexibility
Consensus analyst view is constructive (Buy-rated, ~24% implied upside to average $215 price target) reflecting confidence that 2026 represents a growth trough ahead of reacceleration
bear_case: DISH Wireless/EchoStar's default and Chapter 11 bankruptcy has already removed ~$200M of annualized U.S. revenue and created industry-wide litigation risk over how much more tower revenue could be at risk from tenant network decommissioning

Latin America is a persistent drag (guided -3% in 2026, expected to stay weak through 2027) driven by carrier distress (WOM bankruptcy, AT&T Mexico arbitration) that highlights ongoing emerging-market counterparty risk
High leverage (~$37B total debt) and REIT structure make AMT particularly sensitive to interest rates; rising Treasury yields have repeatedly pressured the stock and raise the cost of refinancing

A meaningful share of the 2026 guidance raise reflects favorable currency translation rather than core operating improvement, a tailwind that could reverse and expose underlying growth as softer than headline numbers suggest

CoreSite, while fast-growing, remains small relative to hyperscale data center peers (Digital Realty, Equinix) and its AI-driven demand surge could prove cyclical if AI infrastructure capital spending decelerates
